title: Absorption by Roots
tagline: Diffusion, osmosis, turgidity, plasmolysis, imbibition and root pressure — how roots take up water and how plant cells behave in solutions.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Water enters a plant through the roots, and the root hair is the main site of absorption. Before explaining how water moves in the plant, this chapter studies the cell processes that make absorption possible: diffusion, osmosis, turgidity and plasmolysis, imbibition and root pressure. These ideas explain why a root hair is suited to its job, how a plant cell gains and loses water, and why wilting, guttation and the movement of water in the plant can be understood in the same framework.

facts.label: Core idea
facts.value: Water enters the root hair by osmosis because the cell sap is more concentrated than the soil water

facts.label: Key processes
facts.value: Diffusion, osmosis, imbibition, turgidity, plasmolysis and root pressure

facts.label: Root hair
facts.value: Thin-walled extension of an epidermal cell with a large surface area and concentrated cell sap

blocks.text: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration until the particles are spread evenly. It happens in gases and in liquids and does not need a membrane. Osmosis is a special case of diffusion in which water moves through a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water concentration, or lower solute concentration, to a region of lower water concentration, or higher solute concentration. A selectively permeable membrane allows water to pass but not large solute molecules. Osmosis is the process most important for water movement into root hairs and for the water balance of plant cells.

items.meaning: Net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration until evenly spread.
Movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane from higher water potential to lower water potential.
Allowing water to pass but not large dissolved molecules.
A measure of how much water tends to move; pure water has the highest water potential.
A dissolved substance that lowers water potential when added to water.

items: Diffusion does not need a membrane; osmosis does.
Osmosis is the movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane.
Water moves from higher water potential to lower water potential.
A solute lowers water potential by making the water less pure.
Osmosis explains water entry into root hairs.
Diffusion and osmosis are passive processes; they do not use energy directly.

items.text: The smell of a flower spreading through a room is diffusion of gases.
items.note: This is a simple example of movement from higher to lower concentration.

items.text: A piece of dried fruit, or a raisin, placed in water swells because water enters by osmosis.
items.note: This is a familiar classroom example of osmosis in a plant tissue.

blocks.text: When a plant cell is placed in water or in a dilute solution, water enters the cell by osmosis. The vacuole fills, the protoplast swells and presses against the rigid cell wall. The cell is then said to be turgid, and the pressure of the contents against the wall is turgor pressure. Turgidity gives support to soft plant parts and helps the plant stay upright. If the cell is placed in a concentrated solution, the opposite happens: water leaves the cell by osmosis, the vacuole shrinks and the protoplast pulls away from the cell wall. This is plasmolysis. A plasmolysed cell loses turgidity and the plant part may wilt. If the cell is returned to water in time, water can re-enter and the cell may recover, but prolonged plasmolysis can damage the cell.

items.meaning: Swollen and firm because the vacuole is full and pressing on the cell wall.
Pressure of the cell contents against the cell wall when the cell is turgid.
Shrinkage of the protoplast from the cell wall when water leaves the cell by osmosis.
Soft and not firm, because the cell has lost turgor.
Loss of firmness in plant parts due to loss of turgidity.

items: A cell gains water and becomes turgid when placed in a dilute solution.
Turgidity presses the protoplast against the cell wall and supports soft tissues.
A cell loses water and becomes plasmolysed when placed in a concentrated solution.
Plasmolysis is the shrinkage of the protoplast from the wall.
Wilting is the visible effect of loss of turgidity in plant parts.
A plasmolysed cell can recover if returned to water in time.

items.text: Leaf cells of a well-watered plant are turgid and the leaves are firm.
items.note: Turgidity is what keeps many herbs and young stems upright.

items.text: A plant in strong fertiliser solution may wilt because the root cells lose water and become plasmolysed.
items.note: This explains one kind of 'fertiliser burn' in simple terms.

blocks.text: Imbibition is the adsorption of water by a solid, such as wood, seeds or cell walls, causing swelling. It is a physical process and does not require a selectively permeable membrane. Imbibition is important in the early stages when dry seeds take up water and in the movement of water into materials that have an affinity for it. Root pressure is a positive hydrostatic pressure developed in the xylem because the root cells actively pump ions into the xylem and water follows by osmosis. Root pressure can push water a short distance up the plant and is shown by guttation in some plants and by bleeding from a cut stem. It is more important in small plants and is not the main force that lifts water in tall trees, where transpiration pull is dominant.

items.meaning: Adsorption of water by a solid, causing swelling.
Positive pressure in the xylem produced by active pumping of ions and the osmotic entry of water.
Exudation of liquid water from leaf margins in some plants, associated with root pressure.
Movement of substances using energy, against a concentration gradient.

items: Imbibition is the swelling of solids by adsorption of water.
Dry seeds imbibe water when placed in it.
Root pressure is a positive push, not a suction.
Root pressure is caused by active uptake of ions and the osmotic entry of water.
Guttation is a visible sign of root pressure in some plants.
Root pressure alone cannot account for the rise of water in tall trees.

items.text: A dry seed soaked in water swells and may even split its coat because of imbibition.
items.note: This is one reason seeds need water to begin germination.

items.text: Some herbs show small droplets at the leaf margins on moist nights, a sign of root pressure.
items.note: Guttation is not dew; it is liquid from inside the plant.

keyPoints: Diffusion is the movement of particles from higher to lower concentration.
Osmosis is the movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane.
A turgid cell is firm because the vacuole presses on the cell wall.
Plasmolysis is the shrinkage of the protoplast from the cell wall in a concentrated solution.
Wilting is caused by loss of turgidity.
Imbibition is the swelling of solids by adsorption of water.
Root pressure is a positive push caused by active ion uptake and osmosis.
Guttation is a sign of root pressure, not dew.
Root pressure supports water movement in small plants but is not the main force in tall trees.

assessment.title: Absorption by Roots: check your understanding
instructions: Answer the short questions in one or two sentences each.
For the long and analytical questions, write in full sentences and name the processes and conditions clearly.
All questions are original practice; they are not past paper questions.

exercises.answer: Osmosis is the movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water concentration, or lower solute concentration, to a region of lower water concentration, or higher solute concentration.
exercises.explanation: The definition should mention water, a selectively permeable membrane and the direction of movement.

exercises.answer: Diffusion is the movement of particles from higher to lower concentration and does not need a membrane. Osmosis is the movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane and is a special case of diffusion.
exercises.explanation: Any clear difference, especially the need for a membrane and the fact that osmosis is water movement, carries the marks.

exercises.answer: Plasmolysis is the shrinkage of the protoplast from the cell wall when a plant cell loses water by osmosis in a concentrated solution.
exercises.explanation: The definition should mention water loss, osmosis and the separation of the protoplast from the wall.

exercises.answer: A plant wilts when its cells lose water and become flaccid due to loss of turgidity, usually because water loss exceeds water uptake.
exercises.explanation: Wilting is due to loss of turgidity from insufficient water in the cells.

exercises.prompt: Define root pressure and give one example of its effect.
exercises.answer: Root pressure is the positive hydrostatic pressure developed in the xylem because root cells actively pump ions in and water follows by osmosis. One example of its effect is guttation, the exudation of liquid water from leaf margins in some plants.
exercises.explanation: The definition should mention active ion uptake and osmotic water entry, and an example should be named.

exercises.answer: Imbibition is the adsorption of water by a solid, such as a seed or wood, causing swelling.
exercises.explanation: The definition should mention adsorption of water by a solid and swelling.

questions.prompt: The movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane is:
questions.explanation: Osmosis is the movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing diffusion — that does not require a membrane.

questions.prompt: When a plant cell is placed in a dilute solution, it becomes:
questions.explanation: In a dilute solution water enters the cell and it becomes turgid.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing plasmolysed — that happens in a concentrated solution.

questions.prompt: The shrinking of the protoplast from the cell wall is called:
questions.explanation: Plasmolysis is the shrinkage of the protoplast from the cell wall.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing turgidity — that is the opposite condition.

questions.prompt: Water enters the root hair by:
questions.explanation: Water enters the root hair by osmosis because the cell sap is more concentrated than the soil water.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing active transport — minerals are actively absorbed, but water moves by osmosis.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of imbibition?
options: Water rising in a plant stem
questions.explanation: A raisin or dried fruit swelling in water is a familiar example of imbibition.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing water rising in a stem — that is mainly due to osmosis and transpiration, not imbibition.

questions.prompt: Root pressure is best described as:
options: A suction force from the leaves
A positive pressure in the xylem
The loss of water from leaves
questions.answer: A positive pressure in the xylem
questions.explanation: Root pressure is a positive pressure in the xylem produced by active ion uptake and osmosis.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing a suction force from the leaves — that describes transpiration pull, not root pressure.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a cell becomes ________ when the vacuole fills and presses on the cell wall.
questions.explanation: A turgid cell has a full vacuole pressing on the wall.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'plasmolysed' — that is the opposite condition.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: guttation is a sign of ________ pressure.
questions.explanation: Guttation is associated with root pressure.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'transpiration' — that is the pulling force, not the push that produces guttation.

questions.prompt: Explain why a plant cell becomes turgid in a dilute solution.
questions.answer: In a dilute solution the water concentration outside the cell is higher than inside the vacuole, so water enters the cell by osmosis through the cell membrane. The vacuole fills, the protoplast swells and presses against the rigid cell wall, and the cell becomes turgid. The cell wall prevents the cell from bursting.
questions.explanation: A good answer mentions osmosis, water entry, vacuole filling and the role of the cell wall.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the cell bursts like an animal cell — the plant cell wall prevents that.

questions.answer: Plasmolysis occurs when a plant cell is placed in a concentrated solution. Water leaves the vacuole by osmosis, the vacuole shrinks and the protoplast pulls away from the cell wall. The cell becomes flaccid and loses turgidity. If the cell is returned to water in time, water may re-enter and the cell may recover.
questions.explanation: A good answer describes water loss, osmosis, the pulling away of the protoplast and the loss of turgidity.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the cell wall shrinks — the wall stays firm, the protoplast shrinks away from it.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a root hair and explain why it is suited to absorption.
questions.answer: A root hair is a thin-walled, single-celled extension of an epidermal cell. It has a large surface area because of its long, narrow shape, and its vacuole contains cell sap that is more concentrated than the surrounding soil water. This concentration difference causes water to enter the root hair by osmosis. The thin wall and large surface area make absorption efficient, and the root hair is positioned in the soil where water is available. The cell also helps the plant absorb minerals, which enter by active transport.
questions.explanation: A strong answer should cover shape, surface area, cell sap concentration, osmosis and mineral uptake.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the root hair stores food — its main role is absorption, not storage.

questions.prompt: A student says that a plant wilts only because it has no water. Is this always true? Give reasons.
questions.answer: No, it is not always true. Wilting occurs when the cells lose turgidity because water loss exceeds water uptake. This can happen not only when soil water is scarce, but also when the plant loses water rapidly in hot, dry or windy conditions, or when roots cannot absorb water because the soil solution is too concentrated, as in over-fertilisation. So wilting depends on the balance between water uptake and water loss, not only on the amount of water in the soil.
questions.explanation: The answer should distinguish lack of water from loss exceeding uptake and mention other causes such as over-fertilisation.
questions.commonMistake: Saying wilting always means the soil is dry — other conditions can cause the same result.
